title: Scaling nutra
summary: How to scale a working COD nutra campaign without breaking it: readiness checks, +20% steps, caps, and the cash you need to survive COD holds. Then how to expand across African, Latin American, European and Asian geos one honest test at a time, and how to manage a portfolio and know when to stop.

lessons.title: When a COD campaign is ready to scale
objectives: By the end you can check whether a COD campaign is truly ready to scale.
By the end you can scale in +20% steps and step back with clear rules.
By the end you can ask a network for a higher cap with data.

steps.p: Scaling a COD campaign multiplies everything: approved leads, but also trash, refusals and cash tied up in holds. If approval or buyout is unstable, more budget turns a small leak into a big loss. In COD, the network's cap, the advertiser's stock and the call centre's capacity can also break before your ads do.

d.b: Scale what is stable, not what is lucky
d.s: Ads, call centre, stock and cash must all be ready.

steps.say: Here's why this lesson matters. Scaling a C O D campaign multiplies everything. More approved leads, yes, but also more trash, more refusals, and more cash tied up in holds. If approval or buyout is unstable, more budget turns a small leak into a big loss. And in C O D, the network's cap, the advertiser's stock, and the call centre's capacity can break before your ads do. So scale what is stable, not what is lucky.

steps.p: All six lines should be true before the first scale step. These are starting lines to adapt. The first is the rule card; the rest protect you from scaling into a wall you cannot see in Ads Manager.
d: Cost per approved ≤ $8.40 with 3+ actual approved
Approval stable within about 5 points for a week
Buyout at or above the network's minimum
Cash reserve covers the bigger spend
steps.say: Here's the readiness check. All six lines should be true before your first scale step, and these are starting lines to adapt. Cost per approved at or under eight dollars forty, with three or more actual approved leads. Approval stable within about five points for a week. Buyout at or above the network's minimum. Trash under your account average. Cap and stock headroom confirmed. And a cash reserve that covers the bigger spend. The first line is the rule card. The rest protect you from scaling into a wall you can't see in Ads Manager.

steps.p: Example: an ad set at $50 a day, raised 20% at each 48-hour checkpoint while it stays at or under the scale line. After six steps it is at about $149 a day. Each step is small enough that delivery usually stays stable.
steps.say: This bar chart shows an example. An ad set starts at fifty dollars a day. At each forty eight hour checkpoint, while it stays at or under the scale line, it's raised twenty percent. Sixty dollars, seventy two, about eighty six, about a hundred and four, and so on. Look at the last bar. After six steps it's at about a hundred and forty nine dollars a day. Each step is small enough that delivery usually stays stable.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt, using payout $14, target $10.50. Judge each checkpoint on actual approved leads with statuses mostly final. Projections can tell you to stop, never to add budget.

rows: Actual ≤ $8.40, 3+ approved, 48 h since last change
Above $14 after $31.50 at the new level
Kill or return to the last good budget

steps.say: Here are the starting rules, using a fourteen dollar payout and a ten dollar fifty target. Judge each checkpoint on actual approved leads, with statuses mostly final. At eight forty or under, with three or more approved and forty eight hours since the last change, raise twenty percent. Between eight forty and ten fifty, hold. Above ten fifty for two checkpoints, step back twenty percent. Above fourteen dollars after thirty one fifty spent at the new level, kill or return to the last good budget. If approval falls five or more points, stop scaling and find the cause. Remember, projections can tell you to stop, never to add budget.

steps.h: Lab: is this ad set ready for +20%?
steps.p: Use actual approved leads as conversions. The ad set spent $63 over 6 days and has 8 approved leads with statuses final. Target CPA is $10.50. Apply the rule card, then check.

d.task: Spent $63, 8 approved (statuses final), target $10.50, 6 days. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.more: Maths: $63 ÷ 8 = $7.88 per approved, under the $8.40 scale line with more than 3 approved. The rule card says +20%. Before you press it, the readiness check still applies: approval stable, buyout fine, cap and cash ready.
steps.say: Time for a lab. Use actual approved leads as conversions. The ad set spent sixty three dollars over six days, and it has eight approved leads with final statuses. The target C P A, cost per acquisition, is ten dollars fifty. Apply the rule card, and decide: kill, hold or scale. Pause and try it, then check your answer. And remember, even when the rule card says scale, the readiness check still applies before you press the button.

steps.p: Raising one ad set's budget is vertical scaling. Adding new ad sets, creatives, placements or regions is horizontal. In COD, horizontal often holds approval better, because one audience pushed too hard brings in less careful buyers.
d: Vertical|+20% steps on a proven ad set
New creatives|fresh angles from Module 3 on the same offer
New audiences|age bands, broad, lookalikes of approved buyers
New regions|courier-covered areas not yet targeted
steps.say: There are two ways to scale. Raising one ad set's budget is vertical scaling, those twenty percent steps on a proven ad set. Adding new things is horizontal: new creatives, with fresh angles from Module three on the same offer. New audiences, like age bands, broad, or lookalikes of approved buyers. New regions the courier covers that you haven't targeted yet. And a new geo, which is the next lesson's playbook. In C O D, horizontal often holds approval better, because one audience pushed too hard brings in less careful buyers.

steps.p: COD offers have limits outside your ad account. A daily cap is the most leads the network accepts from you per day. Past it, leads may be rejected or unpaid. Ask about all three limits before you scale.

cols: What happens if you pass it
rows: What is my cap? How do I raise it?

steps.say: C O D offers have limits outside your ad account. Look at the table. A daily lead cap is the most leads the network accepts from you per day. Past it, extra leads may be unpaid or rejected. Advertiser stock: if it runs short, approved orders wait and buyout falls. Call centre capacity: if it's overloaded, calls get slower and approval drops. The right column shows what to ask the network for each one. Ask about all three before you scale.

steps.p: Managers raise caps for affiliates who show clean data. Send numbers, not hope. Include volume, approval, trash and buyout, and say exactly what you want and when.

messages.text: Hi. Offer 1042 NG: last 14 days 410 leads, 47% approval, 6% trash, buyout 71% on week-1 cohort. Cap is 40 leads a day.
Can we raise it to 70 a day from Monday? Same sources and creatives.
Numbers look good. 60 from Monday, 70 if approval holds for a week.
Deal. I will send an update next Friday.

steps.say: Here's a chat asking a network manager for a cap increase. Notice the first message. It's all numbers: fourteen days of volume, forty seven percent approval, six percent trash, seventy one percent buyout on the week one cohort, and the current cap of forty leads a day. Then a clear ask: seventy a day from Monday, same sources and creatives. The manager offers sixty from Monday, and seventy if approval holds for a week. Managers raise caps for affiliates who show clean data. Send numbers, not hope.

steps.h: Example: what a cap does to your plan
steps.p: Example: your cap is 40 leads a day. At a $4.50 CPL, the most you can usefully spend is $180 a day across the offer. Scaling ad sets beyond that just buys leads the network will not pay for.
steps.say: Here's an example of what a cap does to your plan. Your cap is forty leads a day. At a four dollar fifty C P L, cost per lead, the most you can usefully spend is forty times four fifty, which is a hundred and eighty dollars a day across the offer. At forty five percent approval, that's eighteen approved a day. Scaling ad sets beyond that just buys leads the network won't pay for.

steps.p: These mistakes turn a profitable week into a bad month. Most come from looking only at Ads Manager while the real limits sit with the network, the call centre and your bank account.
steps.say: These mistakes turn a profitable week into a bad month. On the left: doubling budget overnight, scaling on projected approvals, ignoring the daily cap, and scaling the creative with high approval but low buyout. On the right, the fixes: twenty percent every forty eight hours or more, actual approved only, plan spend under the cap, and check buyout by creative first. Most of these mistakes come from looking only at Ads Manager, while the real limits sit with the network, the call centre, and your bank account.

steps.p: More spend means more people see your ads and more reviews by the platform, the network and sometimes regulators. A claim that slipped through at $20 a day is far more likely to be reported at $200. Recheck every scaled ad against the approved claims list.

d.text: New creatives made for scaling need the same claims check and policy check as the first ones. No shortcuts because the offer is working.

A claim that slipped through at twenty dollars a day is far more likely to be reported at two hundred. So recheck every scaled ad against the approved claims list. As the slide says, new creatives made for scaling need the same claims check and policy check as the first ones. No shortcuts because the offer is working.

steps.p: A short list for every 48-hour checkpoint. If any line fails, hold the budget and fix that line first. Log every step with the date, the old and new budget and the reason, so you can undo it cleanly.
d: Actual cost per approved at or under $8.40
Cap headroom for the extra leads
Cash reserve still covers the new spend
Change logged with date and reason
steps.say: Here's your short list for every forty eight hour checkpoint. Actual cost per approved at or under eight forty. Three or more approved, with statuses mostly final. Forty eight hours since the last change. Cap headroom for the extra leads. Cash reserve still covers the new spend. And the change logged with date and reason. If any line fails, hold the budget and fix that line first. Logging the old and new budget means you can undo a step cleanly.

takeaways: Scale only when cost per approved, approval, buyout, trash, cap and cash are all ready.
+20% every 48 hours or more at ≤ $8.40 with 3+ actual approved; step back −20% after two checkpoints above target.
Ask for cap increases with data: volume, approval, trash and buyout.

Cost per approved $7.90 with 5 approved, but approval dropped 7 points this week. Scale?

lessons.title: Cash flow with COD holds
objectives: By the end you can work out your cash gap from approval lag, hold and payment schedule.
By the end you can calculate the cash reserve you need before each scale step.
By the end you can reduce cash risk from holds, payout changes and currency.

steps.h: Why: profitable and still out of cash
steps.p: In COD you pay for ads today and get paid weeks later. A campaign can be profitable on paper and still empty your account, because each scale step adds spend before the first payout arrives. Many affiliates do not fail on bad campaigns; they fail on good campaigns they could not fund.

d.s: Plan the gap between spend and payout before you scale.

steps.say: Here's why this lesson matters. In C O D you pay for ads today and get paid weeks later. A campaign can be profitable on paper and still empty your account, because each scale step adds spend before the first payout arrives. Many affiliates don't fail on bad campaigns. They fail on good campaigns they couldn't fund. So profit is not cash, and you plan the gap between spend and payout before you scale.

steps.p: Example timeline for one day's spend. Every number here varies by network; ask yours and write them in your plan. The total is your cash gap: the days between paying for a lead and receiving its payout.
d: Up to 7 days to weekly payout
steps.say: Follow the timeline for one day's spend. It's an example, and every number here varies by network, so ask yours and write them in your plan. Day zero, the ad spend. About three days until statuses are final. A fourteen day hold. Up to seven days waiting for the weekly payout. And about a day for the transfer to arrive. Add those up and you get your cash gap: the days between paying for a lead and receiving its payout.

steps.p: Add the delays together. In the Example: 3 + 14 + 7 + 1 = 25 days. For those 25 days, every dollar you spend is out of your pocket. Use the worst case for the weekly payout wait, not the best.
steps.say: Here's the formula. Approval lag, plus hold, plus the wait for payout day, plus transfer, equals your cash gap. In the example, three plus fourteen plus seven plus one is twenty five days. For those twenty five days, every dollar you spend comes out of your pocket. And use the worst case for the weekly payout wait, not the best.

steps.p: Example: $200 a day spend and a 25-day cash gap. Before the first payout arrives you will have spent $5,000. Add a 20% buffer for bad days and late payments: $6,000. That is the cash this campaign needs, even if it is profitable.
steps.more: Why a buffer? Payouts can be late, approval can dip, and you may find a winner you want to scale. A 20% buffer is a starting choice. If the network has paid late before, or the hold is long, use more. The formula stays the same: daily spend × cash gap days × buffer.
steps.say: Let's work out the cash you need. Example: two hundred dollars a day of spend, and a twenty five day cash gap. Before the first payout arrives you'll have spent five thousand dollars. Add a twenty percent buffer for bad days and late payments, and you get six thousand dollars. That's the reserve this campaign needs, even if it's profitable. Twenty percent is a starting choice. If the network has paid late before, or the hold is long, use more. The formula stays the same: daily spend, times cash gap days, times buffer.

steps.p: Example: $200 a day at target, which earns about $267 a day in approved payouts. First payout arrives on day 25 for week one's leads. By day 30 you have spent $6,000 and received $1,867. The campaign is profitable; your bank balance is $4,133 lower.
steps.more: Maths: at the $10.50 target, $200 buys about 19.05 approved leads a day ($200 ÷ $10.50), worth 19.05 × $14 = $266.67. Week one's leads (7 days) are worth $1,867 and arrive after the 25-day gap. Week two's payout arrives about a week later. Cash catches up only after the gap; scaling resets the gap for the extra spend.
steps.say: This chart shows the example. Two hundred dollars a day at target earns about two hundred and sixty seven dollars a day in approved payouts. Look at the spend line, climbing steadily. Now the payouts line. It sits at zero until day twenty five, when week one's leads are paid. By day thirty you've spent six thousand dollars and received one thousand eight hundred and sixty seven. The campaign is profitable, but your bank balance is four thousand one hundred and thirty three dollars lower. And scaling resets the gap for the extra spend.

steps.h: Example: how the hold changes your reserve
steps.p: Example at $200 a day. Gap = 3-day approval lag + hold + 7-day wait + 1-day transfer. Longer holds need much more cash. A better payout schedule can be worth more to you than a higher payout.
steps.say: This table shows how the hold changes your reserve, again at two hundred dollars a day. With a seven day hold, the gap is eighteen days and the reserve is four thousand three hundred and twenty. With fourteen days, a twenty five day gap and six thousand. With thirty days, a forty one day gap and nine thousand eight hundred and forty. Longer holds need much more cash. That's why a better payout schedule can be worth more to you than a higher payout.

steps.p: Each scale step needs more cash for the whole gap. Example with a 25-day gap and 20% buffer. Check this before every +20% step; if the reserve is not there, the step waits.
steps.say: Each scale step needs more cash for the whole gap. Here's the example with a twenty five day gap and a twenty percent buffer. At two hundred a day, you need six thousand. At two hundred and forty, seven thousand two hundred. At two hundred and eighty eight, eight thousand six hundred and forty. At three hundred and forty six, ten thousand three hundred and eighty, which is four thousand three hundred and eighty more than you started with. Check this before every twenty percent step. If the reserve isn't there, the step waits.

steps.p: Example: over 30 days you spent $6,000 and earned $8,000 in approved payouts, but only $1,867 has arrived. Work out the profit on paper, then compare it with the cash you actually received.

d.task: Spend $6,000, approved payouts earned $8,000. What is the profit on paper?

steps.more: Maths: $8,000 − $6,000 = $2,000 profit on paper (30 days × $266.67 is about $8,000). Cash received so far is $1,867, so your bank balance is $4,133 lower than when you started. Both numbers are true. Plan with the second one.
steps.say: Time for a lab. Example: over thirty days you spent six thousand dollars and earned eight thousand in approved payouts, but only one thousand eight hundred and sixty seven has actually arrived. First, work out the profit on paper using the calculator on screen. Then compare it with the cash you actually received. Pause and try it, then check your answer. Both numbers are true, but you plan with the cash one.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They exist so a good campaign never forces a bad decision, such as pausing a winner because a card bill is due.

rows: Pause traffic to that network until paid
One network holds over half your unpaid balance
Add a second network before scaling
Get the reason in writing; recheck your target

steps.say: Here are starting rules for cash, to adapt. If your reserve is under daily spend times gap times one point two, don't scale. If a network payment is seven or more days late, pause traffic to that network until you're paid. If one network holds over half your unpaid balance, add a second network before scaling. And if a payout is reduced after the hold, get the reason in writing and recheck your target. These rules exist so a good campaign never forces a bad decision, like pausing a winner because a card bill is due.

steps.h: Ways to shorten the gap honestly
steps.p: Ask, do not assume. Networks set terms by trust and volume. Clean traffic and a steady record are what earn better terms. Bring your trash, approval and buyout numbers when you ask, and ask again every few months.
d: Weekly payouts|ask after a few clean weeks
Shorter hold|ask with your trash and buyout data
Early payout|some networks offer it for a fee; read the terms
Faster method|bank, e-wallet or crypto, if the network supports it
steps.say: Here are honest ways to shorten the gap. Ask for weekly payouts after a few clean weeks. Ask for a shorter hold, with your trash and buyout data. A lower minimum payout means money moves sooner. Some networks offer early payout for a fee, so read the terms. And a faster method, bank, e-wallet or crypto, if the network supports it. Ask, don't assume. Networks set terms by trust and volume, so bring your trash, approval and buyout numbers, and ask again every few months.

steps.p: You may spend in US dollars on a local card and be paid in dollars, local currency or crypto. Each step can cost fees or exchange losses. Card limits for foreign spend have changed often in some countries; check your bank's current rules.
d: Exchange rate|spend and payout rates differ
Card limits|foreign spend caps can change
Payout adjustments|ask if payouts can change after the hold
steps.say: You may spend in U S dollars on a local card and be paid in dollars, local currency, or crypto. Each step can cost you. Look at the four cards. The exchange rate, because spend and payout rates differ. Card limits, because foreign spend caps can change. In some countries they've changed often, so check your bank's current rules. Fees on transfers, conversions and withdrawals. And payout adjustments, so ask whether payouts can change after the hold.

steps.p: If you sell your own products or services and want to accept USDT or BTC directly, a non-custodial checkout keeps the funds in your own wallet. Network payouts still follow each network's own methods. Any compliant crypto checkout works; this is one option.

d: Cash gap written from the network's terms

lessons.title: Africa COD markets
objectives: By the end you can describe the main African COD geos by language, phone format and delivery reality.
By the end you can target only courier-covered regions and judge regions on approved and paid orders.
By the end you can list the regulator questions to ask before running a geo.

steps.h: Why: Africa is many markets, not one
steps.p: Cash on delivery is common across much of Africa because many buyers prefer to see the parcel before paying. But Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, Johannesburg and Douala differ in language, phone formats, couriers, payment habits and rules. Treating them as one market wastes budget and hurts buyout.

d.b: Every geo is its own test
d.s: Language, couriers, payments and rules all change at the border.

steps.say: Here's why this lesson matters. Cash on delivery is common across much of Africa, because many buyers prefer to see the parcel before paying. But Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, Johannesburg and Douala differ in language, phone formats, couriers, payment habits and rules. Treating them as one market wastes budget and hurts buyout. Every geo is its own test.

steps.h: Geo notes: West, East and Southern Africa
steps.p: A starting overview, not market data. Ask your network for current approval, buyout and delivery coverage per geo. Phone formats are the national formats at the time of writing; validate with a maintained library.

rows: English, Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and others
Cards and EFT more common; ask if COD fits

steps.say: This table is a starting overview, not market data. For Nigeria, consider English, Pidgin, Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo, and coverage varies by state. Kenya, English and Swahili, with mobile money very common. Ghana, English, Twi and others, with mobile money common. South Africa has many languages, and cards and E F T are more common, so ask if C O D fits. Cameroon is French and English, mostly French language creatives. North Africa, Arabic and French. The phone formats on screen are national formats at the time of writing, so validate with a maintained library, and ask your network for current approval, buyout and coverage.

steps.p: These shape approval and buyout more than any creative. Ask the network about each one before you launch, and again every month, because courier coverage and rules change.
d: Addresses|landmarks matter; formal addresses are not always used
Courier coverage|big cities first; rural reach varies
Delivery time|longer waits mean more refusals
Payment at door|cash or mobile money, ask which
Phone on delivery day|buyer must be reachable
steps.say: These delivery realities shape approval and buyout more than any creative. Addresses, because landmarks matter and formal addresses aren't always used. Courier coverage, big cities first, with rural reach that varies. Delivery time, because longer waits mean more refusals. Payment at the door, cash or mobile money, so ask which. And the phone on delivery day, because the buyer must be reachable. Ask the network about each one before you launch, and again every month, because coverage and rules change.

steps.say: Which geo next? Expand where most of what you already know still applies. The same language means creatives need less rework. The same advertiser or network means a known call centre and terms. Similar couriers mean similar buyout patterns. Similar rules mean the claims list needs less change. And a healthy margin per lead makes it worth the learning cost. A geo that shares none of these may still work, but plan a bigger test budget and more time.

lessons.title: Portfolio, risk and when to stop
objectives: By the end you can spot concentration risk across offers, networks, accounts and geos.
By the end you can run a weekly portfolio review with clear stop signals.
By the end you can decide when to refresh, pause or drop an offer.

steps.p: A COD business built on one offer, one network, one ad account and one geo can stop overnight: a policy change, a stock problem, a late payment or a banned account. Spreading across a few of each does not raise profit by itself, but it keeps you in business when one piece fails.

d.b: Spread risk before you need to
d.s: A portfolio survives what a single campaign cannot.

steps.say: Here's why this lesson matters. A C O D, cash on delivery, business built on one offer, one network, one ad account and one geo can stop overnight. A policy change, a stock problem, a late payment, or a banned account. Spreading across a few of each doesn't raise profit by itself. But it keeps you in business when one piece fails. A portfolio survives what a single campaign can't.

steps.p: Look at each line and ask what happens if it disappears tomorrow. If the answer is 'everything stops', that is your biggest risk. Fix the biggest one first.
d: One offer|stock, cap or policy change stops all income
One network|late payment freezes most of your cash
One ad account|a restriction stops all traffic
One geo|a rule change closes the market
steps.say: Here's where concentration hides. One offer, where a stock, cap or policy change stops all income. One network, where a late payment freezes most of your cash. One ad account, where a restriction stops all traffic. One geo, where a rule change closes the market. And one creative, where fatigue drops results everywhere. For each line, ask what happens if it disappears tomorrow. If the answer is everything stops, that's your biggest risk. Fix that one first.

By the starting rule of no network over half, you'd grow Network two or add a third before scaling Network one lines. And the Ghana skin care line lost forty dollars, so apply the stop rules before spending more. Both need action this week.

Approval down five or more points for two weeks, stop scaling and ask the network. Buyout under the network minimum, pause the worst sub I Ds, then review. A network payment seven or more days late, pause traffic to that network. Buyer complaints about claims, stop the ad at once and fix it. Check on cohorts old enough to be final. steps.p: These are the mistakes that end operations that were once profitable. None of them show up on a single good day in Ads Manager. They show up in the weekly review, if you run one.

a.title: Common mistakes
items: Holding a fading offer out of hope
Opening extra accounts to dodge restrictions

b.title: Fixes
items: Refresh once, then pause by rule

steps.say: These are the mistakes that end operations that were once profitable. On the left: all money with one network, holding a fading offer out of hope, ignoring buyer complaints, and opening extra accounts to dodge restrictions. On the right, the fixes: spread the unpaid balance, refresh once then pause by rule, treat complaints as a stop signal, and appeal properly and follow platform rules. None of these show up on a single good day in Ads Manager. They show up in the weekly review, if you run one.

steps.h: Compliance: stay honest at every size
steps.p: As you grow, more people see your ads and more buyers hold your promises to account. Complaints, refusals and regulator attention grow with spend. The rules on claims, data and platform policy do not relax when the business gets bigger.

d.text: If buyers say a product did not match your ads, stop those ads and fix the claims before anything else. Never use extra accounts to get around a restriction.

steps.say: A compliance warning. Stay honest at every size. As you grow, more people see your ads, and more buyers hold your promises to account. Complaints, refusals and regulator attention all grow with spend, and the rules on claims, data and platform policy don't relax. As the slide says, if buyers say a product didn't match your ads, stop those ads and fix the claims before anything else. Never use extra accounts to get around a restriction.

steps.p: Run this after the weekly review. It takes ten minutes and is the best protection you have against one bad week becoming a bad year.

Stop signals checked on final cohorts
Cash reserve covers next week's spend

exam.q: Ad set at $9.20 per approved with 6 approved for two checkpoints. Target $10.50. What do you do?
options: Hold the budget; it is above the $8.40 scale line
exam.why: Between $8.40 and $10.50 is the hold band.

exam.q: Cash gap 25 days, spend $240 a day, 20% buffer. What reserve do you need?
A network offers +$2 payout with a 30-day hold, or the current payout with a 7-day hold. You have little cash. Which is often better for you now?
options: The 7-day hold: a shorter cash gap lets you fund and scale safely
exam.why: At $200 a day the 30-day hold needs about $9,840 in reserve vs $4,320. Cash limits growth more than a small payout difference.

exam.q: Nationwide targeting gives $9.52 per approved and 55% buyout. Courier states give $9.20 and 70% buyout. Advertiser break-even buyout 69%. Which do you run?
options: Courier states: similar cost, buyout above break-even
exam.why: Buyout below the advertiser's break-even will cost you the offer. Courier states keep it viable.

exam.q: Geo C pays $30 at 25% approval with a $6.40 CPL. Geo A pays $14 at 45% with a $4.50 CPL. Which has the better margin per lead?
Your cap is 50 leads a day and your CPL is $4.00. An ad set wants to scale past $200 a day total. What do you do?
options: Ask for a cap increase with data before spending past about $200
Split the extra leads across sub IDs
Send extra leads to a second offer without asking
exam.why: Leads past the cap may be unpaid. 50 × $4.00 = $200.

exam.q: Your Mexican ads run 9am to 6pm on a Lagos-time account. What is the problem?
options: Buyers will see the ad in Spanish
They reach buyers about 2am to 11am Mexico time, mostly outside call-centre hours
exam.why: Mexico City is about 7 hours behind Lagos. Schedule in the geo's time.

options: Rewrite to the approved claim; platform approval is not legal approval

options: Refresh again and wait a month
Pause the offer in that geo and ask the network about approval
Move it to a new ad account
exam.why: Two weeks above target after a refresh is the pause line; the approval drop is a second stop signal.
